amadan.story: Come. The two stems barely resemble each other: past umad-, present ā-, which sounds like yā- after mi- or bi-. Persian shouts “umadam!” (literally “I came!”) to mean “Coming!”, as if it has already arrived. “Khosh umadi” (welcome) is literally “you came well.”

imperative.en: come!
come! (polite, or to more than one)
don’t come!
don’t come! (polite, or to more than one)

raftan.story: Go. In the present, the stem rav- shrinks to a single r: miram, I go. In the command, be- becomes bo- because the o in ro pulls the vowel toward itself: boro. Persian likes its vowels to rhyme. The stem makes nouns too: piyāde-ro, the “foot-goer,” is a sidewalk.

imperative.en: go!
go! (polite, or to more than one)
don’t go!
don’t go! (polite, or to more than one)

shodan.story: Become. The busiest verb in the house: it turns an adjective into an event. Boland (tall) + shodan gives “get up,” literally “become tall.” Bidār (awake) + shodan gives “wake up.” Only shodan changes; the adjective stays put. One collision to watch: nashin can mean “don’t become” (to a group) and also “don’t sit.” Context decides.

imperative.en: get up!
get up! (polite, or to more than one)
don’t get up!
don’t get up! (polite, or to more than one)
wake up!
wake up! (polite, or to more than one)
don’t wake up!
don’t wake up! (polite, or to more than one)
become!
become! (polite, or to more than one)
don’t become!
don’t become! (polite, or to more than one)

neshastan.story: Sit. Spoken Tehrani swallows the first syllable of the present stem: mineshinam becomes mishinam. The stem also makes people: shahr-neshin (city-sitter) is a city dweller, and ruz-neshin, the “day-sitter,” is a person stuck at home.

imperative.en: sit!
sit! (polite, or to more than one)
don’t sit!
don’t sit! (polite, or to more than one)

stems.present: hidden in the endings (-am, -i, -e…), or bāsh- for commands

budan.story: Be. A cousin of English “be,” from the same ancient root. In the present it hides: the endings do the work, so khubam means “I’m fine.” It shows itself in the past (budam, I was) and borrows its own word for “not” (nistam, I’m not). To someone who has been working, Persians say “khaste nabāshi”: may you not be tired.

imperative.en: be fine!
be fine! (polite, or to more than one)
don’t be fine!
don’t be fine! (polite, or to more than one)
be happy!
be happy! (polite, or to more than one)
don’t be happy!
don’t be happy! (polite, or to more than one)
be tired!
be tired! (polite, or to more than one)
don’t be tired!
don’t be tired! (polite, or to more than one)

kardan.story: Do, make. Same ancient root as the Sanskrit karma. Persian builds verbs from it like Lego: sabr (patience) + kardan is “wait,” ajale (haste) + kardan is “hurry,” negāh (a look) + kardan is “look.” In these compounds the command usually drops bo-: sabr kon, not sabr bokon.

imperative.en: wait!
wait! (polite, or to more than one)
don’t wait!
don’t wait! (polite, or to more than one)
hurry!
hurry! (polite, or to more than one)
don’t hurry!
don’t hurry! (polite, or to more than one)
look!
look! (polite, or to more than one)
don’t look!
don’t look! (polite, or to more than one)
do!
do! (polite, or to more than one)
don’t do!

didan.story: See. Past did-, present bin-, and that bin is everywhere: durbin (far-seer) is a camera, khoshbin (good-seer) an optimist, badbin (bad-seer) a pessimist. And “didi?!” (did you see?!) is the gossip’s favorite word.

imperative.en: see!
see! (polite, or to more than one)
don’t see!
don’t see! (polite, or to more than one)

khordan.story: Eat. Persians also eat water and tea: āb khordan, chāy khordan. Here the command keeps its bo-, because breakfast and tea are things being eaten, not part of the verb: sobhune bokhor!

imperative.en: eat!
eat! (polite, or to more than one)
don’t eat!
don’t eat! (polite, or to more than one)
eat breakfast!
eat breakfast! (polite, or to more than one)
don’t eat breakfast!
don’t eat breakfast! (polite, or to more than one)
drink tea!
drink tea! (polite, or to more than one)
don’t drink tea!
don’t drink tea! (polite, or to more than one)

dashtan.story: Have. The one everyday verb that refuses mi- in the present: dāram, never midāram. It also runs the “right now” tense: dāram miram, literally “I have going,” means I’m on my way (Day 4). With dust (friend) in front it’s how Persian likes and loves: dust dāram, I like it; dustet dāram, I love you, literally “I have you as a friend.”
dashtan.noImp: No everyday command. To say “keep it,” Persian switches verbs: negah dār (hold).

khastan.story: Want. Spelled with a silent vāv: خواستن is khāstan. A thousand years ago it was said khvāstan, and the spelling never let go; the same ghost vāv sits in khāb (sleep) and khāhar (sister). Speech squeezes the present hard: written mikhāham, Mass says mikhām. In Chapter 4 it learns to pull another verb behind it: mikhām beram, I want to go.
khastan.noImp: Commands of khāstan exist but are rare. You won’t need them.

dunestan.story: Know (a fact). The ān→un rule again: written midānam, Mass says midunam. The family: dānesh (knowledge), dānā (wise), and dāneshgāh, the place of knowledge, a university (Day 4). Knowing a person is a different verb, shenākhtan. Nemidunam (I don’t know) may be the most useful word in this chapter.
dunestan.noImp: Bedun ke… (know that…) exists in speeches and love songs, but you won’t need a command for “know.”

tunestan.story: Can. Written mitavānam shrinks to mitunam. The root tavān means power: tavānā is powerful. The past tunestam means “I managed to,” not “I could if I wanted.” On its own, nemitunam is a full sentence: I can’t.
tunestan.noImp: No command form. You can’t order someone to be able.

goftan.story: Say, tell. Past goft-, present gu-, which Tehrani speech crushes to g-: written miguyam, Mass says migam. You already know mige from “Bābā mige.” Begu! (tell me!) is the gossip’s second favorite word, after didi?!

imperative.en: say!
say! (polite, or to more than one)
don’t say!
don’t say! (polite, or to more than one)

dadan.story: Give. Past dād-, present dah-, which speech softens to d-: written midaham, Mass says midam. Like kardan, it builds verbs from nouns: gush (ear) + dādan = listen, “give ear.” A look-alike word, dād, means a shout: dād nazan! is “don’t yell!”

imperative.en: give!
give! (polite, or to more than one)
don’t give!
don’t give! (polite, or to more than one)
listen!
listen! (polite, or to more than one)
don’t listen!
don’t listen! (polite, or to more than one)
